rv.q: Moments of sheer stage poetry are mixed with effervescent fun.
This is the best British comedy since One Man, Two Guvnors and deserves equal success.
This is a play that stands on its own two feet as a heady celebration of the act of theatre.
But this is a joyous, poignant show, delivered by a crack ensemble and peppered with enjoyable performances: notably David Oakes as an impish Marlowe and Anna Carteret as a canny Elizabeth I.
The glory of the production is Lucy Briggs-Owen.
Like many such beverages, this show is moderately fizzy and leaves a slightly synthetic aftertaste.
It’s funny, romantic and thrilling, dripping with beautiful costumes adorning a huge cast on a simple but stylish set that can be manipulated and lit to create plenty of breathtaking moments.
Both are excellent of their kind, and enough to set anyone well on their way to being in love with Shakespeare.
As Tom Bateman’s unquenchably dynamic Shakespeare reasserts himself, you realize that while the show is hardly newfangled, it’s a big-hearted hit.
Shakespeare in Love proves a fun, clever and enjoyable adaptation of the movie.

cn.t: Critics are mostly charmed by Lee Hall's stage adaptation, praising its wit, energy, and theatrical spirit. Some find the second half overlong and the plot tangled, but the comedy and cast win most over.
